To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ratio of branched-chain amino acids to aromatic amino acids is reduced in the plasma of patients with systemic inflammation.

the ratio of branched-chain to aromatic amino acid concentrations in the brain is decreased in sepsis and that this change is associated with increased brain uptake of the aromatic amino acid phenylalanine and increased net release of glutamine.

(1) during sepsis, the brain increases its net release of glutamine, (2) this release is not caused by an increase in the uptake of amino acids from the plasma, and (3) proteolysis is unlikely to be the cause of this release, because there was no increase in the release of amino acids that are derived from proteolysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the brain in the pathogenesis of sepsis.
the role of proteolysis in amino acid metabolism in sepsis, with a special emphasis on the role of glutamate and glutamine.
the regulation of cerebral proteolysis and the role it plays in cerebral metabolism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
lipopolysaccharides induce a decrease in the brain amino acid pool size.
lipopolysaccharides induce an increased cerebral protein degradation, which leads to increased glutamine release and increased phenylalanine influx.
endotoxin infusion induces a change in the amino acid profile in human brain tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that cerebral proteolysis does occur during endotoxemia, but that it is not the only mechanism responsible for the observed changes in brain amino acid exchange.
we have demonstrated that the human brain is a net consumer of amino acids during systemic inflammation, and that this is mainly caused by the increase in brain glutamine synthesis.
we found a significant increase in net glutamine release during endotoxin-induced sepsis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is an active organ in the septic state, which is not a passive organ.
glutamine is the major source of ammonia in the brain, and the brain is not able to produce glutamine from ammonia.
glutamine release from septic brain is a consequence of a decreased brain uptake of glutamate, not of an increase in brain proteolysis.
